title: Mardana's last song
hook: tradition says when Mardana died, Nanak asked his son Shahzada to carry on playing
tomorrow: The boy who feared the fire

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raja Shivnabh, who waited for Nanak and turned away every imitation. Your line was worth the wait. What did you wait for without grabbing a substitute? Day seven hundred thirty-nine.

A guitar case sits by the door after the funeral. Nobody wants to open it. Everybody knows what's inside: the strings he tuned, the pick still tucked under them. Somebody, someday, has to decide what happens to it. All along this path, when Nanak sang, a rabab played beside him, in the hands of Mardana, the Muslim musician who walked the long roads with him. In the sakhis, he was there at the strange cities, the hunger, the bitter fruit. Today the music changes hands. Rabab.
screen: `A GUITAR CASE BY THE DOOR.` → `MARDANA'S RABAB.` → `THE MUSIC CHANGES HANDS.`

segments.voice: Tellings disagree about where Mardana died. Some place it on the road, far to the west; some at Kartarpur, near the end of Nanak's travels. What they share is the shape. Tradition says that as Mardana grew weak, Nanak sat with him and asked what he wished for his body, whether he wanted a tomb raised over him, as was done for honored men. And Mardana, the story goes, said no. Why trap me in a tomb of stone, when you've freed me from the tomb of the body? In some tellings, Nanak and his Sikhs then sang hymns for him, and Nanak told the family not to wail but to sing the Lord's praise. Then comes the turn. Tradition says Nanak called Mardana's son, Shahzada, and asked him to take up the rabab and keep playing. Look at what this ending keeps. A friendship that never asked Mardana to stop being who he was: a Muslim musician and a Guru, side by side to the end. Look, too, at what doesn't get built. No monument. The memorial is the music. And the sound didn't stop with one man. Sikh tradition remembers rababis, rabab players descended from Mardana, playing kirtan in the courts of later Gurus. Then there's the son. Grief can make the music stop. In this story, the comfort Nanak gives is a job: pick it up, and play.
screen: `TELLINGS DIFFER ON WHERE.` · `NO TOMB OF STONE.` · `SHAHZADA TAKES THE RABAB.` · `THE MEMORIAL IS THE MUSIC.` · then, large: `KEEP PLAYING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank a musician. Use the sit to choose one. A singer who carried you through a hard year. The person who leads the hymns where you worship. A grandparent who hummed while cooking. A kid down the street learning trumpet badly and bravely. Let the sound come back to you for a moment. Then decide how you'll say thank you today: a message, a coin in a case, a word after the service. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath. The bell holds the time.
Rabab, the instrument Mardana played to the end of his life, when, tradition says, he refused a tomb and Nanak gave it to his son Shahzada.
Your line: keep playing. Today, pick back up one small good thing someone you loved used to do, and do it once. Day seven hundred thirty-nine.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember Bhai Mardana as Guru Nanak's companion and rabab player, and the rabab and the rababi tradition of kirtan are honored in Sikh music.
